title: Guess Number Higher or Lower II
summary: In the Guessing Game, you must guess a number between 1 and n.
statement: In the Guessing Game, you must guess a number between 1 and n. For each incorrect guess, you pay an amount in dollars equal to the guessed number. You win by guessing the correct number, but you lose if you run out of money. Determine the least amount of money needed to ensure a win, regardless of the number I choose.
constraints: 1 <= n <= 200. The hidden integer is in [1,n]. A wrong guess x costs x; a correct guess costs nothing.
Return the minimum budget that guarantees success in the worst case. This is an ordinary function problem; no interactive guess API is used.
hints: The cost of a strategy is its worst hidden-number outcome, not its average number of guesses.
For every interval, try each first guess and combine its cost with the worse remaining interval.
dp[l][r]=min(g+max(dp[l][g-1],dp[g+1][r])) over g in [l,r]. Singleton intervals cost zero.
Fill shorter intervals before longer ones. Minimizing the worst branch yields a guaranteed budget.
editorial: A wrong first guess splits the remaining candidates into lower and upper intervals. The adversary may choose the more expensive branch, so use their maximum; then minimize over the first guess. A singleton requires no paid mistake. Bottom-up interval DP evaluates all choices. The independent small-input oracle enumerates every binary decision tree and simulates every hidden number. Larger deterministic cases are cross-checked separately by a top-down minimax implementation.

tests.explanation: A strategy starting at 7 needs at most 16: the upper branch may pay 7 then 9, while the lower branch can be solved within 8 more. No strategy guarantees a smaller budget.
There is only one possible number. Guess it correctly and pay nothing, so the answer is 0.
